Senses.Explanation: The literal image of a withered or dry tree, deployed in several fixed phrases. In the crone-burning-the-hermitage case, the attendant embraces the hermit and asks what it is like. He answers, 'A withered tree leans against a cold cliff; through three winters there is no warm air.' The crone rejects his answer and burns the hermitage. 'Withered-tree hall' is a hall name and location, as in 'before the withered-tree hall, gibbons cry and tigers roar.' In the Xiangyan case, 'What is the Way?' receives 'a dragon hums inside a withered tree,' and 'Who is the person in the Way?' receives 'eyes inside a skull.' Hongzhi later comments, 'It may be called a withered-tree dragon hum—still carrying joy; eyes in a skull—still carrying consciousness.' Other recurring compounds are 'flowers on a withered tree,' 'withered tree and cold cliff,' and 'withered-tree Chan.' The image also forms an institutional epithet: Shishuang's biography says that students sat for long periods without lying down and stood rigid like stumps, so throughout the realm they were called the withered-tree assembly. These are separate attested phrases built from the same tree image.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide image with multiple fixed deployments. Current counts: withered tree 1,752/295 files; dragon hums inside a withered tree 108/39; withered-tree dragon hum 91/62; eyes inside a skull 97/37; flowers on a withered tree 106/67; withered-tree hall 63/42; withered tree leans against a cold cliff 47/43; withered tree and cold cliff 24/23. The crone-burning-the-hermitage and Xiangyan passages are raised cases and remain occurrence-key null. Hongzhi's appraisal is his own commentary. The withered-tree assembly is an institutional label distinct from the hall name and the dragon-hum phrase. The crone's rejection is recorded as part of that case, not made into a second lexical meaning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 枯木倚寒巖，三冬無煖氣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (永覺元賢禪師廣錄); the (婆子燒庵) case retold — (正恁麼時如何)？(主曰)：(枯木倚寒巖)，(三冬無煖氣)，after which the crone burns the hut. Raised/stock case, MasterName null. (Same phrase recurs at 0568c02 in this file, count=2.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 嚴曰。枯木裏龍吟。曰。如何是道中人。嚴曰。髑髏裏眼睛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), within (撫州曹山本寂禪師) section, a raised case naming Xiangyan: (僧問香嚴)。(如何是道)。(嚴曰)。(枯木裏龍吟)…(髑髏裏眼睛) — (嚴) = (香嚴智閑). Raised case, MasterName null; the words are Xiangyan's. Pairs (枯木裏龍吟) with (髑髏裏眼睛).

Occurrences.Kwic: 可謂枯木龍吟。猶帶喜在。髑髏眼睛。猶帶識在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (宏智禪師廣錄), Hongzhi's own commentary: (可謂枯木龍吟)。(猶帶喜在)。(髑髏眼睛)。(猶帶識在)。(直是智不到處) — Hongzhi (Caodong) turning the (枯木龍吟)/(髑髏眼睛) pair. Master's own record.
(建中靖國續燈錄), (潭州石霜崇勝院法永禪師) upper-hall: (霜華臺上)，(翠色回環)；(枯木堂前)，(猨啼虎嘯) — (枯木堂) as a locus in a parallel couplet. MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 學眾有長坐不臥。屹若株杌。天下謂之枯木眾也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元), in the biography of Shishuang Qingzhu's community: 'among the students were those who sat for long periods without lying down, standing rigid like stumps; throughout the realm they were called the withered-tree assembly' (學眾有長坐不臥。屹若株杌。天下謂之枯木眾也).

Senses.Explanation: To violate or transgress a binding precept. The compound occurs 40 times in 31 allowlisted Chan texts. In a public case attributed to Jingshan, a person who has cultivated good all his life once violates the precept against taking what was not given; the passage then supplies an explicit naming formula: ‘the one who violates a precept is immediately named a thief’ (犯戒者即名為賊). Another recorded interview poses the opposed pair, ‘a precept-keeping monk does not ascend to heaven; a precept-violating monk does not fall into hell—what do you say?’ (持戒比丘不上天堂，犯戒比丘不落地獄，汝作麼生？). The Caoshan record quotes a former teacher saying, ‘to set the mind is to violate a precept; to acquire a taste is to break the fast’ (擬心是犯戒，得味是破齋), then repeats that taking pleasure in the ‘flavor of buddhas and ancestral teachers’ is violating a precept. Linquan quotes an ancient saying that neither honors people merely for keeping the fast and precepts nor slights them merely for breaking them, while still calling keeping them a monastic's own duty and breaking them the ground of an ordinary person. These are attested expansions and contrasts around the same violation category, not grounds for erasing the hard rule or for deciding why the records apply it as they do.
Senses.Note: Flyswatter-test deviation: an actual precept violation becomes the named status in public interview and is directly contrasted with keeping; the Caoshan passage also applies the category to setting the mind and acquiring a taste. ‘Violate a precept’ (犯戒) is narrower than ‘break the precepts’ (破戒): both denote violation in these records, but this entry preserves the corpus's explicit naming formula and does not claim a technical distinction not stated by the passages. The ordinary violation, public-interview comparison, Caoshan re-grounding, and quoted keep/break appraisal all concern what counts as violation rather than different referents, so the entry remains one corpus-wide sense. Exact count: 40 hits in 31 files.

Occurrences.Kwic: 善者一日偶犯不與取戒，惡者一念了悟自心。犯戒者即名為賊，了悟者即名為佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Jingshan case names the violated rule as the precept against taking what was not given and directly calls the violator a thief.

Occurrences.Kwic: 持戒比丘不上天堂，犯戒比丘不落地獄，汝作麼生？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question directly contrasts a precept-keeping monk with a precept-violating monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 先師曰。擬心是犯戒。若也得味是破齋。且喚什麼作味。只是佛味祖味。纔有忻心便是犯戒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Caoshan record quotes a former teacher: setting the mind is violating a precept, acquiring a taste is breaking the fast, and taking pleasure in the flavor of buddhas and ancestral teachers is violating a precept. Because the immediate words belong to an unnamed former teacher, MasterName remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古德有語云：我見持齋守戒者亦不敬，我見破齋犯戒者亦不輕。何也？持齋守戒者，出家本分事也；破齋犯戒者，凡夫地面也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linquan quotes an ancient saying that neither honors a person merely for keeping the fast and precepts nor slights one merely for breaking them, while naming keeping them a monastic's own duty and breaking them the ground of an ordinary person. The quoted speaker is unnamed.

Senses.Explanation: In its primary Zen-loaded use, Handan names the imitator in the stock verdict “Handan learns the Tang gait” (邯鄲學唐步), attested 43 times in 31 allowlisted files; the shorter “learn the Handan gait” (邯鄲學步) occurs eight times in seven. Jingqing applies the verdict when a monk walks away after being asked how he understands Zhaozhou’s “drink tea”; Xuedou then asks, “this monk is not a Handan man—why does he learn the Tang gait?” (這僧不是邯鄲人，為甚學唐步). Other instructions attach it to uneven footing, warn that turning inside verbal sequences invites ridicule as “Handan learning to walk,” and speak of “losing the patch-robed monk’s nose and forgetting Handan’s former gait” (打失衲僧鼻孔，忘却邯鄲故步). Chan thus turns the place-name into a stock person/type and verdict in case commentary and direct appraisal. The corpus’s explicit walking, gait, and imitation language controls this target.
Senses.Note: This person/type differs from the actual place and the personal title below. Variants with “Tang gait,” “learn to walk,” and “former gait” belong to one imitation family, not separate readings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 清云：邯鄲學唐步。雪竇顯云：這僧不是邯鄲人，為甚學唐步？
脚下若參差，邯鄲學唐步。
不可在語脈裡轉嫫母效顰邯鄲學步見笑大方取譏識者
打失衲僧鼻孔，忘却邯鄲故步。

Senses.Explanation: The graphs also name the actual city of Handan. One verse says, “my home is in Handan” (妾家邯鄲住). Chan writing also preserves the city as the setting of the yellow-millet dream: “one pillow at Handan: he passed through fifty years of glory; on waking, the yellow millet was not yet cooked” (邯鄲一枕，歷盡榮華五十載，覺來黃粱炊尚未熟). Literal residence and the dream’s setting retain the same geographic referent; the literary allusion does not make a new place.
Senses.Note: This sense covers the place itself, including when a poem invokes the dream located there. It is secondary because the imitation formula dominates the Chan concordance.

Occurrences.Kwic: 妾家邯鄲住，歌聲亦抑揚
邯鄲一枕，歷盡榮華五十載，覺來黃粱炊尚未熟

Senses.Explanation: In one biographical passage, “Handan” is part of a personal title rather than the city or imitator: “the Duke of Handan, personal name Shu, was then seven years old” (邯鄲公諱淑，時方七歲). The title identifies the named child in that retrospective.
Senses.Note: This distinct title/person use has one allowlisted source and is therefore provisional. It is not merged into the geographic sense merely because the title contains the place-name.
